title: Finite-grid Gram contraction: roundoff, range and a certified normalizer
question:
Work over the real numbers. Let \(n\ge0\), let \(d_0=d_n=1\) and \(d_j\ge1\), and let the two slices \(A_j^0,A_j^1\in\mathbb R^{d_{j-1}\times d_j}\) of core \(j\) be supplied dyadic rationals. Their denominators divide \(2^{b_{\rm in}}\), and every entry has magnitude at most a supplied \(M_j\ge0\). For an ordered bit word \(s\in\{0,1\}^n\), put \(x_s=A_1^{s_1}\cdots A_n^{s_n}\), a scalar. An empty product is 1 and there is one empty word. You may use, without re-proving, the exact Gram identity
\[
E_n=[1],\qquad E_{j-1}=\sum_{t=0}^1 A_j^t E_j(A_j^t)^T,
\qquad (E_0)_{11}=\sum_s x_s^2=\|x\|_2^2.
\]

Here is a particular finite-grid algorithm, not a floating-point black box. Choose an integer \(b\ge b_{\rm in}\), use the grid \(h\mathbb Z\) with \(h=2^{-b}\), and let \(Q_b\) round to a nearest grid point with any fixed tie convention; hence \(|Q_b(z)-z|\le u=h/2\). Inputs, 0 and 1 are represented exactly. Set \(\widehat E_n=[1]\). At step \(j\), with \(m=d_j\), compute, separately for each \(t\), \(\widehat T^t\) by multiplying \(A_j^t\widehat E_j\) with the following dot-product schedule: start the accumulator at 0, round each scalar product with \(Q_b\), then round every addition into the accumulator. In the same way compute \(\widehat S^t\) from \(\widehat T^t(A_j^t)^T\), and set each entry of \(\widehat E_{j-1}\) to \(Q_b(\widehat S^0+\widehat S^1)\). Do not impose symmetry or positivity on the rounded environment. Initially reason on the unbounded grid; a finite signed range will be chosen from your intermediate-value bounds.

1. With \(\|F\|_{\max}=\max_{a,c}|F_{ac}|\), derive a uniform error certificate for this schedule. In particular, prove that the safe constants
\[
L_j=2d_j^2M_j^2,\qquad R_j=4d_j^2M_j+4d_j+1
\]
permit \(e_n=0\) and \(e_{j-1}\le L_j e_j+uR_j\), where \(e_j=\|\widehat E_j-E_j\|_{\max}\). Derive an explicit unrolled bound \(e_0\le uC_0\), and specify a backwards recurrence for all \(C_j\). Tighter constants from exact grid additions are also acceptable if every later bound is updated consistently. Bound the magnitudes of stored environments, both kinds of scalar products and all partial sums, and explain how finitely many integer bits can be chosen to prevent overflow. A range bound for only the final scalar is insufficient.

2. Let an independent certificate supply \(\|x\|_2\ge\mu>0\). When the rounded scalar \(\widehat s=(\widehat E_0)_{11}\) is positive, take one correctly rounded square root \(\widehat r=Q_b(\sqrt{\widehat s})\). Derive explicit sufficient conditions for \(\widehat s>0\) and \(\widehat r>0\), and a quantitative bound on
\[
\left\|\frac{x}{\widehat r}-\frac{x}{\|x\|_2}\right\|_2.
\]
The numerator \(x\) and the displayed divisions are exact mathematical quantities here; output-coordinate rounding and a circuit implementation are not included. For any requested \(\varepsilon>0\), give a sufficient inequality on \(u\), and therefore an integer choice of \(b\ge b_{\rm in}\), that establishes both positivity facts and error at most \(\varepsilon\), without first assuming those positivity facts. State why \(x/\widehat r\) need not have norm exactly one.

3. Check \(n=0\), zero cores and zero mass with correctly scoped premises. For any fixed \(b\ge2\), give a legal one-core grid input with nonzero exact mass whose computed \(\widehat s\) is zero. Explain what this says about a guarantee without a lower-mass/precision margin, and why the exact-real Gram identity or an exact-real operation count alone is not the finite-grid certificate proved here. No claim about optimal constants, bit-operation runtime, core-generation error or quantum gate synthesis is requested.

assumptions: Finite real scalar-boundary train with strictly positive bond dimensions and exact supplied dyadic core entries.
A known finite magnitude bound M_j for each core and an integer input precision b_in; working b is at least b_in.
The precise Q_b multiplication/addition schedule in the question; nearest-grid rounding has absolute error at most u=2^(-b-1).
The normalization branch separately receives an independent true-norm lower bound mu>0; the raw-error branch does not assume positive mass.
The correctly rounded square root is invoked only after positivity of its input has been established.
conventions: Core products are ordered left-to-right by emitted bit; real transpose, entrywise maximum matrix norm and Euclidean vector norm are distinct.
There is one empty word; an empty product is one. All environment matrices have positive dimensions.
Q_b has a fixed tie rule; all stored grid additions are actually exact on an unbounded grid, but charging u for them yields the requested conservative certificate.
x/r_hat is an exactly divided mathematical vector; no output amplitude rounding, input-core generation error, circuit or bit-runtime claim is included.

mathematical_target: Derive a finite-grid two-pass Gram error and range certificate, then establish a positive rounded normalizer and an explicit precision guarantee from an independent mass margin; exhibit a legal small-mass failure.
reference_answer:
Write \(m=d_j\) and \(M=M_j\) within a single update. The arithmetic analysis concerns the supplied rounded algorithm. The exact Gram semantics in the question is a separate supplied interface.

First consider a scheduled dot product of length \(m\) with exact operands \(a_k,z_k\) at that call. Write \(p_k=Q_b(a_kz_k)=a_kz_k+\alpha_k\) and \(q_k=Q_b(q_{k-1}+p_k)=q_{k-1}+p_k+\beta_k\), with \(q_0=0\) and \(|\alpha_k|,|\beta_k|\le u\). Induction gives
\[
q_m-\sum_{k=1}^m a_kz_k=\sum_{k=1}^m(\alpha_k+\beta_k),
\qquad\left|q_m-\sum_{k=1}^m a_kz_k\right|\le2mu.
\]
The operands may themselves be outputs of earlier rounded calls: the bound is relative to their current stored values. On this unbounded fixed grid, each addition is in fact exact, so \(\beta_k=0\). Keeping the displayed conservative bound is legitimate and gives the constants requested.

For each bit \(t\), write
\[
\widehat T^t=A_j^t\widehat E_j+F^t,
\qquad \|F^t\|_{\max}\le2mu,
\]
\[
\widehat S^t=\widehat T^t(A_j^t)^T+G^t,
\qquad \|G^t\|_{\max}\le2mu.
\]
There are \(m\) terms in every dot product of both passes; the left bond size affects how many entries there are, not the error bound for one entry. The final addition introduces a matrix \(H\) with \(\|H\|_{\max}\le u\). Therefore
\[
\widehat E_{j-1}=\sum_t A_j^t\widehat E_j(A_j^t)^T+Z_j,
\quad Z_j=\sum_t[F^t(A_j^t)^T+G^t]+H.
\]
For one bit, \(\|F^t(A_j^t)^T\|_{\max}\le m(2mu)M\). Summing both bits gives
\[
\|Z_j\|_{\max}\le(4m^2M+4m+1)u=uR_j.
\]
Neither symmetry nor positive semidefiniteness of \(\widehat E_j\) was used.

For an arbitrary error matrix \(D\), each entry of \(A_j^tD(A_j^t)^T\) is a sum of \(m^2\) terms, each bounded by \(M^2\|D\|_{\max}\). Hence
\[
\left\|\sum_tA_j^tD(A_j^t)^T\right\|_{\max}
\le2m^2M^2\|D\|_{\max}=L_j\|D\|_{\max}.
\]
Subtract the exact update from the rounded update to obtain \(e_{j-1}\le L_je_j+uR_j\); the exact terminal identity gives \(e_n=0\). Define
\[
C_n=0,\qquad C_{j-1}=L_jC_j+R_j.
\]
Backward induction yields \(e_j\le uC_j\), with
\[
C_j=\sum_{k=j+1}^{n}R_k\prod_{\ell=j+1}^{k-1}L_\ell,
\qquad C_0=\sum_{k=1}^{n}R_k\prod_{\ell=1}^{k-1}L_\ell.
\]
All factors are nonnegative. The empty-product convention is essential: the residual produced at step 1 reaches the final scalar with coefficient one. No division by an \(L_j\) is used, so zero core bounds cause no singular formula.

Here is a range certificate for the same algorithm. Define
\[
B_n=1,\qquad B_{j-1}=L_jB_j+uR_j.
\]
Assuming \(\|\widehat E_j\|_{\max}\le B_j\), a rounded first-pass product has magnitude at most \(MB_j+u\). Its first \(k\) accumulated terms have magnitude at most \(kMB_j+2ku\), so every first-pass entry is bounded by
\[
F_j^{\rm range}=mMB_j+2mu.
\]
A rounded second-pass product is bounded by \(MF_j^{\rm range}+u\); its first \(k\) accumulated terms by \(kMF_j^{\rm range}+2ku\). Thus every second-pass entry is bounded by
\[
G_j^{\rm range}=mMF_j^{\rm range}+2mu.
\]
The final addition has magnitude at most \(2G_j^{\rm range}+u=B_{j-1}\). This closes the induction for the environment envelope. The exact pre-round products are bounded by \(MB_j\) and \(MF_j^{\rm range}\). A pre-round accumulator at its \(k\)-th addition is bounded by the corresponding displayed partial-sum bound (in fact its bound saves one \(u\)); the pre-round bit-sum is bounded by \(2G_j^{\rm range}\). Thus the bounds cover operands, products and all sums, not just \(\widehat s\).

Let \(K\) be the maximum of 1, all input bounds \(M_j\), all \(B_j\), \(M_jB_j+u\), \(F_j^{\rm range}\), \(M_jF_j^{\rm range}+u\), \(G_j^{\rm range}\), and \(\sqrt{B_0}+u\). The last term covers the square-root output when its input is nonnegative. There are finitely many finite terms. Choose an integer \(I\ge0\) with \(2^I>K+h\) and represent stored grid numbers in \([-2^I,2^I-h]\). Every scheduled value then lies strictly inside this range, so overflow cannot occur. Exact scalar products before rounding may use a widened temporary with \(2b\) fractional bits; that is a representation requirement, not a unit-cost bit-operation assertion. This range argument concerns the explicit multiply/add schedule and the input/output contract of the correctly rounded square-root primitive; it does not specify the internal algorithm or cost of that primitive.

For the normalization branch put \(r=\|x\|_2\), \(s=r^2\), and \(\Delta=uC_0\). The scalar Gram interface and the preceding bound give \(|\widehat s-s|\le\Delta\). If \(\Delta<\mu^2\), then
\[
\widehat s\ge\mu^2-\Delta>0.
\]
The square root is therefore defined on a positive argument. Rationalizing the difference gives
\[
|\sqrt{\widehat s}-r|
=\frac{|\widehat s-s|}{\sqrt{\widehat s}+r}
\le\frac{\Delta}{\sqrt{\mu^2-\Delta}+\mu}.
\]
After rounding the square root, set
\[
\theta=\frac{\Delta}{\sqrt{\mu^2-\Delta}+\mu}+u.
\]
Then \(|\widehat r-r|\le\theta\). If additionally \(\theta<\mu\), then \(\widehat r\ge\mu-\theta>0\), and exact division gives
\[
\left\|\frac{x}{\widehat r}-\frac{x}{r}\right\|_2
=r\left|\frac1{\widehat r}-\frac1r\right|
=\frac{|r-\widehat r|}{\widehat r}
\le\frac{\theta}{\mu-\theta}.
\]
The produced mathematical vector has norm \(r/\widehat r\), so a rounded normalizer generally does not give exact unit norm. The bound concerns rescaling error of the same numerator, not a claim about a different state direction or a physical circuit output.

One explicit precision choice establishes its own positivity premises. For \(\varepsilon>0\), define
\[
\tau=\frac{\varepsilon\mu^2}{(1+\varepsilon)(C_0+\mu)}>0
\]
and choose \(u\le\tau\). Since \(C_0\ge0\) and \(\mu>0\), this implies
\[
\Delta\le\frac{\varepsilon\mu^2 C_0}{(1+\varepsilon)(C_0+\mu)}<\mu^2.
\]
Thus \(\widehat s>0\) is proved before the square-root bound is invoked. Moreover
\[
\theta\le\frac\Delta\mu+u
=u\left(\frac{C_0}\mu+1\right)
\le\frac{\varepsilon\mu}{1+\varepsilon}<\mu.
\]
Consequently \(\widehat r>0\), and monotonicity of \(z/(\mu-z)\) for \(0\le z<\mu\) gives error at most \(\varepsilon\). Equivalently, a sufficient working precision is
\[
b\ge\max\left\{b_{\rm in},0,\left\lceil\log_2\frac1{2\tau}\right\rceil\right\}.
\]
This follows from \(u=2^{-b-1}\); the maximum with zero handles \(2\tau>1\). Once this \(b\) is selected, recompute the finite range envelope with that \(u\). The supplied core bounds \(M_j\) and therefore \(C_0\) do not depend on this subsequent precision choice.

For \(n=0\), the single amplitude, exact environment, rounded environment and rounded square root all equal 1; every error is zero. The recurrence has \(C_0=0\), and the conservative \(u\)-term in the general square-root bound need not be attained. If a nonempty chain has an identically zero core, then that update produces an exactly zero rounded environment, and all earlier updates remain zero; the exact mass is also zero. More generally, zero exact mass means every \(x_s=0\), so \(x/\|x\|\) is undefined. The raw-error theorem still applies, but the normalization branch's premise \(\mu>0\) with \(r\ge\mu\) cannot hold. No zero-mass example is claimed to satisfy that branch.

For the requested nonzero failure take \(n=1\), \(d_0=d_1=1\), \(b_{\rm in}=b\ge2\), \(A_1^0=[h]\) and \(A_1^1=[0]\). The first pass returns \(h\) exactly. The second pass rounds \(h^2\) to zero, because \(0<h^2<h/2\); its additions and the final bit-sum remain zero. Thus \(x=(h,0)\) has exact mass \(h^2>0\), but \(\widehat s=0\). The lower-mass/precision margin is deliberately not satisfied. Positivity alone supplies no uniform safe fixed precision over arbitrarily small masses. This legal schedule witness, and the local error/range analysis above, distinguish the finite-grid result from the supplied exact identity or an exact-real operation count. No supplier accuracy, bit runtime or gate synthesis is inferred.

rubric.criterion: Derives the dot-product rounding error and both matrix-pass residuals, correctly counting m terms per pass; obtains R_j=4m^2M+4m+1 or a rigorously justified tighter constant. Award 0.5 for the dot product, 1 for propagation of first-pass error through the transposed core, and 0.5 for two bits/final sum. Merely quoting a generic floating-point theorem does not establish this schedule.

Derives L_j=2m^2M^2 from the entrywise double sum (0.5), establishes the backward recurrence with exact terminal error zero (0.5), and unrolls C_0 with products of earlier indices and valid empty products (0.5). No division by L_j is permitted without a separate zero case.

Provides a noncircular backwards environment magnitude envelope (0.5), bounds both kinds of products and all partial sums/pre-round values (1), and selects a finite signed range including the square-root input/output with sufficient precision for temporary products (0.5). Only bounding the final scalar earns at most 0.5 here.

Uses the independent mu bound to prove positivity of s_hat from a strict squared-mass margin (0.5); derives a square-root perturbation bound with the rounding error included (0.5); proves r_hat positive before division (0.5); and obtains the exact rescaling-error identity and a valid quantitative bound, noting non-unit norm (0.5). Do not demand the reference rationalization form if an equivalent justified bound is supplied.

Gives an explicit u condition and integer b choice that independently imply all positivity and epsilon-error premises, in that order. Award 1 for a correct sufficient condition with its strictness proof and 0.5 for a correct logarithmic/integer precision conversion respecting b_in. A circular appeal to assumed positivity does not earn the first point.

Computes a legal one-core nonzero grid input that rounds to zero (0.5), and handles n=0/zero mass with scoped premises plus the exact-real versus finite-grid/circuit boundary (0.5). A valid alternative counterexample and a general boundary argument receive equal credit.

common_errors: Using an operator-norm bound as if it were the entrywise maximum norm, omitting the m^2 factor.
Forgetting that first-pass rounding is multiplied by the transposed core in the second pass.
Unrolling the backwards recursion with later rather than earlier L factors.
Claiming rounded environments remain PSD or assuming the computed mass is positive before checking a margin.
Applying the square-root or reciprocal formula at a zero/nonpositive computed scalar.
Giving a precision implication that quietly retains the strictness premise it was supposed to prove.
Treating exact fixed-grid additions as worse than their stated upper error bound invalidates no estimate, but claiming every addition necessarily incurs u is false.
Claiming a grid error certificate is a bit-runtime theorem or a unitary implementation.

boundary_cases.resolution: The unique amplitude and both exact/rounded normalizers are 1; C_0=0, exact error zero.
Both exact and rounded final mass vanish; raw-error analysis applies, but positive-mass normalization assumptions are incompatible.

boundary_cases.case: Zero exact mass without a positive certificate
boundary_cases.resolution: The target normalized vector is undefined; no normalization conclusion is made.

boundary_cases.case: A working precision too coarse for the mass
boundary_cases.resolution: The one-core h input at b>=2 has mass h^2>0 yet rounds to zero; it deliberately fails the sufficient margin.
The sum/product recurrence stays defined, with no division by L_j.
Grid additions are exact, so valid tighter constants and consistent derived thresholds are accepted.

Exact Gram update and E_0(1,1)=||x||^2, explicitly supplied in the question.
Specified two-pass Q_b schedule, |Q_b(z)-z|<=u, terminal identity exact, and correctly rounded sqrt only on a nonnegative input.
For the precision branch only, requested epsilon>0; choose b respecting b_in.

steps.claim: Bound a scheduled dot product relative to its stored operands.
steps.conclusion: Error <=2m u; partial error is the sum of multiplication/addition rounding terms.
steps.justification: Expand q_k=q_{k-1}+a_k z_k+alpha_k+beta_k and sum. The grid makes additions exact, but the conservative bound remains valid.
First-pass error is multiplied by A^T; sum its m M amplification, second-pass error and final addition over two bits.

steps.claim: Propagate environment error through the exact local map.
steps.justification: Bound each of the two m-by-m index sums by m^2 M_j^2 e_j and subtract the exact recurrence.

steps.conclusion: C_n=0, C_{j-1}=L_j C_j+R_j, e_j<=u C_j, C_0=sum_k R_k product_{ell<k}L_ell.
steps.justification: Backward induction and finite distributivity; no division by potentially zero L_j.

steps.conclusion: B_n=1, B_{j-1}=L_j B_j+uR_j bounds environments; first products/partial sums <=M_j B_j+u / k M_j B_j+2ku, and analogous second-pass bounds use F_j=m M_jB_j+2mu.
steps.justification: Use the current environment envelope as an operand bound; bound both pass accumulators before closing the next environment bound.

steps.claim: Choose a finite representable range without overflow.
steps.conclusion: Finite K covering inputs, all products, sums, environments and sqrt input/output allows 2^I>K+h and range [-2^I,2^I-h].
steps.justification: The finite list of bounds is finite. Widen temporary products to retain 2b fractional bits before rounding. This does not specify a bit runtime or internal sqrt algorithm.

assumptions: The two strict inequalities are antecedents of the stated implication, not globally assumed facts.
steps.conclusion: IF Delta=uC_0<mu^2, s_hat>0 and theta=Delta/(sqrt(mu^2-Delta)+mu)+u bounds |r_hat-r|. IF also theta<mu, r_hat>0 and the rescaled-vector error is <=theta/(mu-theta).
steps.justification: First lower-bound s_hat, then rationalize the square-root difference, add its rounding error, establish positive r_hat, and only then divide.

steps.claim: Make precision supply the strict margins.
steps.conclusion: Choosing u<=tau=epsilon mu^2/((1+epsilon)(C_0+mu)) gives Delta<mu^2 and theta<=epsilon mu/(1+epsilon)<mu; b>=max(b_in,0,ceil(log2(1/(2tau)))) suffices.
steps.justification: C_0>=0 and mu>0 give strictness directly. Define theta only after proving Delta<mu^2. No positive computed mass or rounded norm is presupposed.

steps.claim: Apply the conditional interface after precision supplies its antecedents.
steps.conclusion: Both rounded scalars are positive and the exact rescaling error is at most epsilon.
steps.justification: AND join: quantitative error interface plus independently produced strict margins; monotonicity of z/(mu-z).

steps.claim: Check unconditional empty and zero-core arithmetic boundaries.
steps.conclusion: n=0 gives exact scalar/sqrt 1 and error zero; an identically zero core gives exact and rounded final mass zero.
steps.justification: Use the empty product or Q_b(0)=0 throughout the schedule. The raw theorem has no positive-mass premise.

steps.claim: Separate zero mass from the normalization domain.
assumptions: Replace the positive-mass branch by r=0; do not retain G1-I4.
steps.conclusion: If exact mass is zero, every coordinate is zero and normalization is undefined; no mu>0 lower certificate can then hold.
steps.justification: Finite nonnegative sum of squares and the definition of normalization.

steps.claim: Construct a nonzero input that loses mass under rounding.
assumptions: Retain the raw arithmetic model; do not impose the sufficient precision margin of G1-S8.
steps.conclusion: For n=1, A^0=h,A^1=0,b_in=b>=2, x=(h,0) has positive mass but s_hat=0.
steps.justification: First pass gives h; 0<h^2<h/2 makes the second-pass product round to zero, independently of ties.

reasoning_map.AND_join_policy: Every required_inputs list is conjunctive. G1-S7 is an implication; G1-S8 proves its antecedents independently, and G1-S9 is the application. Zero-mass and coarse-precision diagnostics explicitly replace or omit the normalization/precision branch premises.

reused_results.assessment: Supplied, not re-assessed as the prior C3 exact Gram theorem.

reused_results.external_overlap: E1 has a separate operator-residual certificate using the same elementary recurrence topology; no independent-scoring clearance.

reconvergent_branches.why: Rounded local residual and exact local update jointly determine total error.
A conditional analytic interface needs a separately established strict nonzero margin.

overlap.assessed_delta: Specified finite-grid schedule, local roundoff constants, intermediate range certificate and noncircular mass-to-bit-precision guarantee.

existing_core_comparisons.relation: Same exact two-pass Gram schedule; existing target proves an exact-real operation count. No rounded-value or range theorem is assessed there.
Exact scalar norm and marginal exact sqrt/read cost are shared context. G1 assesses numerical positivity, rounded sqrt and sufficient finite-grid precision.
Exact normalization domain is shared; the sum-of-squares identity is supplied rather than re-assessed.

prior_cohort_comparisons.relation: The exact scalar Gram identity is explicitly supplied. G1 adds arithmetic-model analysis, not another proof of cross-Gram semantics.
Shared need for a positive mass margin. G1 compares the same exact numerator with a rounded scalar normalizer, not perturbation of vector direction.
Both propagate a raw numerical error to a normalization condition; C4 uses Bernstein coefficients and an exact norm, while G1 derives error from a local stored arithmetic schedule.

current_batch_comparisons.relation: Shared elementary backwards recurrence/unrolling and norm-margin logic; E1 starts from operator residual certificates and assesses downstream state/circuit/postselection composition. G1 owns finite-grid schedule/range/bit analysis.
